data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy": null, "claim": "The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's terms as a non-inductive, methodological rule of 'critical rationality' that maximizes exposure to falsification, not probability of truth.", "counterconditions": [{"case": "If the preference implies an expectation that the future will resemble the past (induction), it fails.", "checker_spec": null, "eval": "observation"}, {"case": "If 'acting on' a theory requires believing it is probably true, the defense collapses.", "checker_spec": null, "eval": "observation"}, {"case": "If the Tichý/Miller critique of verisimilitude removes all non-probabilistic grounds for preference.", "checker_spec": null, "eval": "observation"}], "definitions": [], "derivation": [], "formalization_refs": [], "mechanism": "Popper distinguishes between logical probability (which he rejects for corroboration) and methodological utility. The preference is a decision to subject our conjectures to the severest possible tests. Choosing the theory with higher empirical content (and thus higher corroborability) is the only way to learn faster, even if it doesn't make the theory more likely to be true. It is a pragmatic imperative for growth of knowledge, not an inductive inference about the future.", "premises": [], "schema": "deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1", "scope": {"covers": [], "excludes": []}, "simulation_refs": [], "uncertainties": []}
